questions.question: What is OpenClaw?

options.text: An AWS managed service for monitoring
An open-source AI agent that runs locally and connects tools via skills

explanation.correct: OpenClaw is an open-source AI agent that runs locally on your machine and connects messaging channels (WhatsApp, Slack, Telegram) to skills you define.
explanation.why: A is CloudWatch/AWS Health. C is a separate product. D is not a real product.

questions.question: In OpenClaw, what is a 'skill'?

options.text: A folder containing a SKILL.md and scripts that tell the agent what to do

explanation.correct: A skill is a single folder with a SKILL.md (which the agent reads to understand the task) and scripts it can execute.
explanation.why: A, C, D are AWS-native constructs — not OpenClaw concepts.

questions.question: Which AWS SDK clients are used in the aws-health OpenClaw skill?

explanation.correct: The aws-health skill uses @aws-sdk/client-ec2, @aws-sdk/client-ecs, and @aws-sdk/client-cloudwatch.
explanation.why: The skill monitors compute infrastructure (EC2, ECS) and pulls metrics via CloudWatch.

questions.question: What IAM permission level should the OpenClaw IAM user have?

options.text: Read-only access for specific services only
Write access to EC2 and ECS

explanation.correct: OpenClaw only needs to read and return data. Never grant write access — read-only for EC2, ECS, and CloudWatch is sufficient and safest.
explanation.why: Principle of least privilege: the agent only reads infra state. Write access creates unnecessary risk.

questions.question: What TypeScript runner does the aws-health skill use (no build step required)?

explanation.correct: The skill uses 'tsx' as the TypeScript runner, which eliminates the need for a separate build step.
explanation.why: tsx runs TypeScript files directly, making development and deployment simpler.

questions.question: Which messaging channels does OpenClaw support for triggering skills?

explanation.correct: OpenClaw supports WhatsApp, Slack, and Telegram as messaging channels that can trigger skill execution.
explanation.why: The session demo used WhatsApp, but Slack and Telegram are also supported.

questions.question: What does the aws-health skill return when queried for EC2?

options.text: Only the count of running instances
Instance name, type, AZ, state, system status check, and CPU 15-min average (EC2); running vs desired tasks, deployment state, last 5 stopped tasks (ECS)
Security group rules and VPC configurations

explanation.correct: EC2: instance name, type, Availability Zone, state, hardware system status check, and CPU utilization 15-minute average from CloudWatch. ECS: all clusters/services, running vs desired task count, deployment rollout state, and the last 5 stopped tasks with stop reasons.
explanation.why: It uses DescribeInstances and DescribeInstanceStatus for EC2, then GetMetricStatistics from CloudWatch for CPU.

questions.question: What is the minimum Node.js version required for the aws-health OpenClaw skill?

explanation.correct: The aws-health skill requires Node.js 18 or higher.
explanation.why: Node 18 introduced native fetch and other improvements used by modern AWS SDK v3.

questions.question: What CLI argument does the aws-health script accept to check only EC2?

options.text: ec2 as a positional CLI argument

explanation.correct: You pass 'ec2' as a positional CLI argument. Passing 'ecs' checks only ECS. Passing nothing checks both.
explanation.why: The script reads process.argv to determine which services to query.

questions.question: Why should you never use root AWS credentials for OpenClaw?

options.text: Root credentials don't work with the AWS SDK
Root credentials cannot access EC2 or ECS APIs
Root credentials have unrestricted access — a compromise would be catastrophic

explanation.correct: Root credentials have full access to every AWS service. If OpenClaw were compromised, an attacker could destroy or modify your entire infrastructure.
explanation.why: Always create a dedicated IAM user with least-privilege read-only access for agents.

questions.question: What is the primary security concern with running a shared OpenClaw instance for multiple users?

options.text: The AI model becomes less accurate with more users
Users share the same file system, breaking user isolation
Costs scale non-linearly with user count

explanation.correct: The core security problem is that multiple users share the same file system and process — there is no isolation between users, which means one user could potentially access another's data or context.
explanation.why: This was the quiz question asked at the session: user isolation breaks down with a shared OpenClaw instance.

questions.question: What is the purpose of SKILL.md in an OpenClaw skill folder?

options.text: A file the AI agent reads to understand what the skill does and when to invoke it
IAM policy definition in YAML format

explanation.correct: SKILL.md is read by the OpenClaw agent (not the developer) — it defines the skill name, description, and when the agent should activate it.
explanation.why: Think of it as an instruction set for the AI about when and how to call this skill.

questions.question: Which AWS API call does the skill use to get the state and metadata of EC2 instances?

explanation.correct: The skill uses DescribeInstances (for metadata: ID, type, name) and DescribeInstanceStatus (for running/stopped/impaired state).
explanation.why: These are the standard EC2 describe APIs. There is no 'GetEC2Health' or 'ListInstances' API.

questions.question: What is the difference between AWS Health API and the aws-health OpenClaw skill?

options.text: AWS Health API gives service-level events; the skill gives granular per-instance/per-cluster metrics
The skill is better for all use cases
AWS Health API requires Enterprise Support

explanation.correct: AWS Health API reports service-level events (e.g., 'EC2 degraded in us-east-1'). The OpenClaw skill gives per-instance state, CPU metrics, ECS task counts — more granular operational data.
explanation.why: An audience member raised this comparison. Both are complementary tools.

questions.question: What environment variables does the aws-health skill expect?

explanation.correct: The skill expects ACCESS_KEY (access key ID), SECRET_KEY (secret access key), REGION, and SESSION_TOKEN variables.
explanation.why: These map to programmatic IAM credentials. The skill reads them to authenticate with the AWS SDK.

questions.question: What analogy did the speaker use to describe OpenClaw's role?

options.text: A database that stores your infra state
Jarvis from Iron Man — a conversational assistant that surfaces infra status on demand
A cron job that sends daily reports
An auto-scaling policy that reacts to health events

explanation.correct: The speaker compared OpenClaw to Jarvis — you ask 'what's going on?' and it tells you the dashboard, statistics, and what's wrong with your production environment.
explanation.why: This framing captures the key value: conversational AI access to your infrastructure state.

questions.question: Which AWS service did the audience suggest as an alternative to polling EC2 describe APIs?

explanation.correct: An audience member asked why not use AWS Health API instead of direct EC2 describe calls — since Health API already exposes service and resource health events.
explanation.why: The speaker acknowledged the suggestion, noting the skill gives more granular per-instance data.

questions.question: What does the skill do if you run it with no CLI arguments?

options.text: Returns an error asking for a service name

explanation.correct: Running the script with no arguments triggers both the EC2 and ECS checks, returning a combined health report.
explanation.why: Passing 'ec2' limits to EC2; passing 'ecs' limits to ECS; no argument runs both.

questions.question: What Python optimization was suggested by the audience for faster health checks?

options.text: Use asyncio instead of sync calls
Use threads to parallelize EC2 and ECS checks

explanation.correct: An audience member suggested using Python threads to run EC2 and ECS queries in parallel, reducing total latency — especially useful for large clusters.
explanation.why: Currently the checks run sequentially. Parallel threads would make it faster for production environments with many instances.

questions.question: What is the architectural flow when a user sends a WhatsApp message to OpenClaw?

options.text: WhatsApp → OpenClaw (local) → SKILL.md → Script → AWS APIs → Response
WhatsApp Business API → SNS → SQS → OpenClaw

explanation.correct: The message goes to OpenClaw running locally on your machine. OpenClaw reads SKILL.md, executes the script, which calls AWS APIs (EC2, ECS, CloudWatch), and returns the structured response back to WhatsApp.
explanation.why: OpenClaw runs locally — it is not hosted in AWS. It uses your machine to make AWS API calls.

questions.question: What does the 'reservations' field in EC2 DescribeInstances response represent?

options.text: A grouping construct wrapping instances launched together

explanation.correct: The reservations field in DescribeInstances is a legacy grouping — it wraps instances that were launched together. The skill iterates through reservations to get to actual instance data.
explanation.why: Common confusion: 'reservation' here is NOT the same as Reserved Instances pricing.

questions.question: What IAM actions are minimally required for the aws-health skill?

explanation.correct: The minimal required actions are the specific describe/list/get calls the scripts use — no wildcards, no write access.
explanation.why: Least privilege: only grant exactly what the agent needs. The iam-policy.json in the repo codifies these exact permissions.

questions.question: What happens if OpenClaw has no running ECS clusters when the skill executes?

options.text: The script throws an unhandled exception
It returns an empty/zero state for ECS — no clusters or tasks found
It defaults to checking EC2 only
It creates a default cluster automatically

explanation.correct: The script handles empty cluster lists gracefully — if no clusters exist, it reports zero clusters/tasks. The speaker demonstrated this live during the session.
explanation.why: Defensive coding: always handle the empty-list case to avoid null pointer errors.

questions.question: What is the key difference between OpenClaw and a traditional monitoring dashboard?

options.text: OpenClaw is conversational — you ask in natural language; no browser or dashboard needed

explanation.correct: The core differentiator is conversational access — instead of opening a browser, logging into CloudWatch, and navigating dashboards at 2am, you type a WhatsApp message and get the answer instantly.
explanation.why: This maps to the '2am production outage' scenario the speaker opened with.

questions.question: If the OpenClaw agent produces an unexpected response, what should you check?

options.text: Check the OpenClaw gateway logs to trace what the agent executed

explanation.correct: Check the OpenClaw gateway logs to see exactly what the agent called, what parameters it passed, and what was returned — this is the debugging path for unexpected agent behavior.
explanation.why: This was the answer to the final quiz question at the session about handling unexpected agent responses.

questions.question: What concept is an OpenClaw skill most analogous to in modern AI frameworks?

options.text: A tool or function in MCP (Model Context Protocol) or agent tool-use

explanation.correct: Skills in OpenClaw are equivalent to tools/functions in MCP or agent frameworks — they define a capability the AI can invoke, with a structured description of when to use it.
explanation.why: An audience member at the end made this connection: MCPs are capabilities, skills are capabilities.

questions.question: Where does OpenClaw run in the described architecture?

options.text: Locally on the developer's own machine
A managed SaaS cloud hosted by OpenClaw

explanation.correct: OpenClaw runs locally on your own machine. It is not deployed to AWS — it uses your machine to make outbound calls to WhatsApp and to AWS APIs.
explanation.why: This is the key architectural point: it's a local agent, not a cloud-hosted service.

questions.question: What is the output format specified in SKILL.md for the aws-health skill?

options.text: JSON to be stored in S3
Structured plain-text report presented to the user as-is via the messaging channel

explanation.correct: The SKILL.md specifies that the script prints a structured plain-text report, and the agent sends it back to the user exactly as-is through the messaging channel (WhatsApp/Slack/Telegram).
explanation.why: No transformation layer — the script output is the message the user receives.

questions.question: What is the purpose of iam-policy.json in the aws-health repo?

options.text: It deploys IAM resources via CloudFormation
It contains the minimal read-only IAM policy to attach to the OpenClaw IAM user
It configures the OIDC provider for the skill

explanation.correct: iam-policy.json contains the exact least-privilege IAM policy with only the specific read actions the skill needs — making it easy to create the correct IAM user without guessing permissions.
explanation.why: Best practice: ship the policy alongside the skill so users can set up IAM correctly.

questions.question: To add RDS monitoring to the aws-health skill, what is the minimal additional IAM action required?

explanation.correct: rds:DescribeDBInstances is the standard API call to get RDS instance status, engine, class, and availability — the minimal read-only permission needed to monitor RDS health.
explanation.why: The speaker mentioned adding RDS as a future enhancement. rds:* would be over-privileged; DescribeDBInstances is the specific action needed.
